subject: religious-studies
title: The Atonement Workshop
welcome_lead: Step into the workshop where theologians from Anselm to Abelard fashion models of how the cross reconciles humanity to God.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on models of the atonement.
final_note: No single image exhausts the mystery the cross is meant to express.

concepts.def: The reconciliation of humanity to God achieved through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
An early model (e.g. Origen, Gregory of Nyssa) in which Christ's death is the price paid to liberate humanity from the devil's power.
Anselm's account in Cur Deus Homo (1098), in which Christ's death satisfies the infinite debt of honour owed to God by human sin.
Peter Abelard's view that Christ's death moves humanity to repentant love by demonstrating God's love.
The Reformation view that Christ bore the legal punishment for human sin in our place.
Gustaf Aulen's 1931 retrieval of the patristic view that the cross is Christ's victory over sin, death, and the devil.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In Cur Deus Homo (1098), Anselm argued that human sin offends God's infinite honour, creating a debt only humanity ought to pay but only God can pay.

Only the God-Man, Jesus Christ, can make satisfaction. His voluntary death pays the debt and restores the moral order of the universe.

Peter Abelard (c. 1079-1142), responding to Anselm, emphasised that Christ's death demonstrates the depth of God's love and so kindles repentant love in humanity.

Critics worry that this reduces the cross to subjective moral persuasion, but it captures a vital New Testament theme.

Gustaf Aulen's Christus Victor (1931) argued that the classical patristic view of the atonement is a dramatic narrative of God's victory over hostile powers, neither legal (Anselm) nor merely moral (Abelard).

The cross and resurrection together defeat sin, death, and Satan, liberating humanity for new life.
